draft.title: Deseasonalising data
card: Seasonal effects can hide the trend. Deseasonalising removes them so we can see whether values are really rising or falling.
To deseasonalise, divide each value by the seasonal index for its season. Deseasonalised value = actual value ÷ seasonal index.
Example: sales are 120 in a season with index 1.2. The deseasonalised value is 120 ÷ 1.2 = 100. This is what sales would be in an average season.
A season with an index below 1 gets adjusted upwards. Sales of 72 with index 0.8 give 72 ÷ 0.8 = 90.
draft.remember: Divide by the seasonal index to take the season out and reveal the trend.

a.q: Ice cream sales in Cairns are 150 boxes in a quarter with a seasonal index of 1.25. What is the deseasonalised value?
a.why: Deseasonalised value = 150 ÷ 1.25 = 120. Multiplying gives 187.5, which adds the seasonal effect instead of removing it.
a.clue: Removing a season's effect means dividing, not multiplying.

b.q: A bookshop in Bendigo sells 210 books in a month with seasonal index 0.70. After deseasonalising, what does this value show?
b.why: 210 ÷ 0.70 = 300. The month is below average, so removing the season raises the value above 210. The 147 comes from multiplying by 0.70 instead.
b.clue: An index below 1 means the month was weaker than average.
